why: A period that was never archived must never be purgeable. Without this, an open period -- one still accepting uploads -- could be destroyed.
expectFailing: refuses a period that was never archived

why: Documents inside the retention window must survive, and an instance with no window configured must refuse everything rather than treating 'unset' as 'keep nothing'.
expectFailing: refuses a period inside the retention window

why: A single file under legal hold blocks its whole period. This is the guard with legal consequences if it silently stops working.
expectFailing: refuses when a file in the period is under legal hold

why: Placing or lifting a legal hold must require the periods.manage permission, not merely reach into the file's directory. Without this, anyone who can view a directory could freeze or unfreeze its files' purge eligibility.
expectFailing: refuses a caller with directory access but no periods.manage

why: A live directory beneath a trashed one must never be listed as viewable, no matter where the grant that would otherwise reach it hangs -- on a live ancestor above the trashed node, or on the trashed node itself. Without this, trashing a directory does not hide the files beneath it, which defeats the point of trashing it.
expectFailing: excludes a live descendant of a trashed directory from viewableDirectoryIds

why: view() must refuse outright when a file's directory was cascade-trashed, not resolve it withTrashed() and fall back on the normal grant. A trashed subtree is already invisible to browsing and search (DirectoryAccess::resolveViewable()); letting view() see through that with a grant that predates the trash would reopen exactly the reveal trashing a directory exists to close.
expectFailing: refuses to view a file whose directory is cascade-trashed, even with access that would otherwise allow it

why: update() must refuse outright when a file's directory was cascade-trashed. Editing a file's metadata in place inside a trashed subtree is the same reveal-and-modify that view() refuses, and without this guard the call falls through to DirectoryAccess::can() with a null directory, which either throws or, if that ever stopped throwing, would need a real answer -- refusing outright is the deliberate one.
expectFailing: refuses to update a file whose directory is cascade-trashed, even with access that would otherwise allow it

why: move() must refuse outright when a file's source directory was cascade-trashed, even when the caller has access to the destination. move() assumes a live file in a live tree; without this guard a grant on the destination alone could move a file out of a trashed subtree, which is restore()'s job, not move()'s.
expectFailing: refuses to move a file whose source directory is cascade-trashed, even with access to a live destination

why: legalHold() must refuse outright when a file's directory was cascade-trashed, even for a periods.manage holder. The view-reach requirement above exists so a capability holder with no reach into a directory learns nothing about what is in it; resolving withTrashed() here would turn the hold check itself into a side channel around exactly that.
expectFailing: refuses a legal hold on a file whose directory is cascade-trashed, even for a periods.manage holder with access

why: A file under legal hold must never be permanently deleted through the single-file purge door. PeriodPurger already blocks a whole period containing one; without this, that hold could be routed around one file at a time.
expectFailing: refuses to purge a file under legal hold

why: A file whose period is archived must never be purged one file at a time. Archived periods are read-only, the same rule RestoreFile and StoreFileVersion already enforce, and the only sanctioned way to reclaim an archived period's storage is the retention-gated PeriodPurger.
expectFailing: refuses to purge a file whose period is archived

why: SQLite's own default busy timeout is zero: the loser of a write race fails immediately instead of waiting. The single container has four writers on one file (FrankenPHP, two queue workers, the scheduler), with queue, cache and session all on the database driver. Remove the stated value and the connector skips the pragma entirely -- back to zero, silently. Scope, corrected after issue #121: this entry used to claim the stated timeout fixes the "General error: 5 database is locked" seen on the jobs table. It does not on its own. A DEFERRED transaction takes no lock at BEGIN, and SQLite refuses a read-then-write outright rather than calling the busy handler, so the timeout never applies to the queue worker reserving a job. That needed transaction_mode IMMEDIATE, which is stated alongside these and asserted by the container smoke. busy_timeout is necessary and was never sufficient.
expectFailing: waits rather than failing when the embedded database is locked

why: Without WAL, a SQLite reader blocks every writer for the length of its read. Laravel leaves journal_mode null, which means the driver's rollback-journal default, so remove the stated value and the pragma is never issued -- the contention this fixes comes straight back, and the suite's own ":memory:" connection cannot see it.
expectFailing: journals the embedded database in WAL mode so readers do not block writers

why: item/files-actions-ui (issue #101): renaming a file through the panel must require edit access, and RenameFile itself never checks -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). Without this the Rename control would work for a viewer holding view alone.
expectFailing: refuses to rename a file without edit access

why: item/files-actions-ui (issue #101): moving a file through the panel must require edit access on both the source and the chosen destination, and MoveFile itself never checks either. Without this the Move control would relocate any file anywhere for any signed-in user.
expectFailing: refuses to move a file without edit access on both ends

why: item/files-actions-ui (issue #101): trashing a file through the panel must require files.delete and edit access, and TrashFile itself never checks. Without this the Trash control would soft-delete any file for a viewer holding view alone.
expectFailing: refuses to trash a file without edit access

why: item/files-actions-ui (issue #101): setting or clearing a legal hold through the panel must require periods.manage, not merely directory reach -- SetLegalHold itself never checks. Without this the control would let anyone who can open the file freeze or unfreeze its purge eligibility, which is exactly what depending on item/legal-hold was supposed to buy here.
expectFailing: refuses to set a legal hold without periods.manage, even with manage access on the directory

why: item/files-actions-ui (issue #101): renaming a directory through the panel must require edit access, and RenameDirectory itself never checks. Without this the Rename control would work for a viewer holding view alone.
expectFailing: refuses to rename a directory without edit access

why: item/files-actions-ui (issue #101): moving a directory through the panel must require directories.manage and manage access, and MoveDirectory itself never checks. Without this the Move control would relocate any directory's subtree for any signed-in user.
expectFailing: refuses to move a directory without directories.manage, manage access alone is not enough

why: item/files-actions-ui (issue #101): trashing a directory through the panel must require directories.manage and manage access, and TrashDirectory itself never checks. Without this the Trash control would cascade-delete any directory's subtree for a viewer holding view alone.
expectFailing: refuses to trash a directory without directories.manage, manage access alone is not enough

why: A trashed file must never be resurrected into the search index. deleted() forgets the projection inline, but a reindex dispatched BEFORE a trash can run AFTER it -- the dispatch from the upload, or an ExtractText still in flight -- and index() is an updateOrCreate, so without this guard the row comes back and the trashed file answers searches again. Trashing is how a person hides something; an index that keeps serving it defeats the point. The suite cannot see this on its own because QUEUE_CONNECTION is sync, which is why the test stages the ordering explicitly and why the container found it first.
expectFailing: does not resurrect a trashed file when a reindex lands after the trash

why: item/files-versions-replace (issue #102): replace() must refuse outright when a file's directory was cascade-trashed, the same as view()/update()/move()/legalHold(). Without this, a grant that predates the trash would let a new version be written into a file inside a subtree that browsing and search already treat as invisible -- writing where nobody can see is the same reveal-and-modify those four methods already refuse, and Replace would reopen it.
expectFailing: refuses to replace a file whose directory is cascade-trashed, even with access that would otherwise allow it

why: item/files-versions-replace (issue #102): replace() must refuse a file that is itself trashed, separately from whether its directory is. StoreFileVersion::handle() finds a file by (directory_id, name_key) through the default, non-trashed query, so for a trashed file it takes the CREATE path and writes a fresh file under the same name -- StoreFileVersionTest's 'does not resurrect a trashed file of the same name' proves that is the action's designed behaviour. A later RestoreFile would then collide on that name, and the trashed original becomes unrestorable. Refusing here is what keeps restore-then-replace the only route.
expectFailing: refuses to replace a trashed file, live directory, full access

why: item/file-policy-trashed-file-guards (issue #116): update() must refuse a file that is trashed on its own, independently of whether its directory is live. Before this, update() only ever asked liveDirectory()'s question and never the file's own trashed() question, so a grant on a live directory could edit metadata on a file already sitting in the trash -- the same reveal-and-modify replace() already refuses for a new version.
expectFailing: refuses to update a trashed file, live directory, full access

why: item/file-policy-trashed-file-guards (issue #116): move() must refuse a file that is trashed on its own, independently of whether its source and destination directories are live. Before this, move() only ever asked liveDirectory()'s question about the source, never the file's own trashed() question, so a grant on both ends could relocate a file already sitting in the trash.
expectFailing: refuses to move a trashed file, live source and destination, full access

why: item/file-policy-trashed-file-guards (issue #116): legalHold() must refuse a file that is trashed on its own, independently of whether its directory is live. Before this, legalHold() checked periods.manage and liveDirectory() but never the file's own trashed() question, so a periods.manage holder with directory access could freeze or unfreeze purge-eligibility on a file already sitting in the trash.
expectFailing: refuses a legal hold on a trashed file, live directory, periods.manage and full access

why: item/files-versions-replace (issue #102): replacing a file through the panel must require files.upload and edit access, and StoreFileVersion itself never checks -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). Without this the Replace control would let anyone who can open the file's detail panel overwrite it with a new version.
expectFailing: refuses to replace a file without files.upload

why: item/files-list-sort-select (issue #103): bulk trash must re-authorise every selected id through FilePolicy::delete, and TrashFile authorises nothing on its own -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). Without this pass the Trash-selected control would soft-delete every file in the directory for a viewer holding view alone. The entry deliberately claims less than the item's wording does: delete() is a global permission plus directory access with no per-file component, so every file in one directory answers identically for one user and a 'one of several refused' case cannot be constructed at all. What is provable is that removing the pass lets a view-only member trash the lot, and that is what the named test asserts. The two-pass authorise-then-trash structure stays regardless, because a single loop would leave the files before a refusal already trashed.
expectFailing: refuses a bulk trash for a viewer without edit access, and trashes nothing

why: A version id that belongs to a different file must 404, never redirect to that file's object. {version} carries no directory_id of its own to check against the viewer's reach, so without this abort_if() anyone who can view ANY file could download the bytes of ANY version in the instance merely by guessing its id -- the cross-file hole authorize('download', $file) alone cannot close, because it only ever asks about $file, never about which file $version actually belongs to.
expectFailing: 404s a version id belonging to a different file

why: item/directory-access-ui (issue #14): granting directory access through the panel must require manageAccess() (Manage-level directory_access), and GrantDirectoryAccess itself checks nothing -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). Without this the Grant control would let anyone who can merely view or edit a directory hand access to it to any other user.
expectFailing: refuses to grant access server-side for a caller without manage access

why: item/directory-access-ui (issue #14): revoking directory access through the panel must require manageAccess() (Manage-level directory_access), and RevokeDirectoryAccess itself checks nothing -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). Without this the Revoke control would let anyone who can merely view or edit a directory strip any other user's access to it.
expectFailing: refuses to revoke access server-side for a caller without manage access

why: item/directory-access-ui (issue #14): directoryGrantsQuery() -- the query BOTH revokeAccess() and render()'s grants listing resolve a grant through -- must scope to the directory currently being managed. Without this, a manager of ONE directory could revoke a grant belonging to a DIFFERENT directory they hold no access to at all, merely by naming its id -- the same cross-resource hole FileVersionDownloadController's cross-file 404 guard closes for versions.
expectFailing: refuses to revoke a grant belonging to a different directory

why: item/directory-access-ui (issue #14): manageAccess() gates grant/revoke, and spec §5 groups "grant/revoke access, move or delete the directory itself" as ONE capability -- move(), delete() and restore() all require directories.manage and this one did not. MEMBER_PERMISSIONS carries no directories.manage, and spec §5 also says every user holds manage on their own home directory by ordinary grant, so without this layer every member could hand anyone any level on their own subtree while being refused the move and delete the same sentence groups with it. It was unreachable only because nothing in the UI called the ability; this item is what makes it live.
expectFailing: requires BOTH directories.manage and a manage-level grant to grant access

why: item/trash-view (issue #15): viewableTrashedDirectoryIds() must narrow the trashed directories it returns to ones the viewer's own access, resolved through can(), actually reaches. Without this filter every trashed directory in the instance -- including one belonging to a user with no grant on it at all -- would be handed to the Trash page's query, which is exactly the leak the item's doneWhen ('another user's trashed items never appear, asserted at query level') exists to close.
expectFailing: excludes a trashed directory the viewer holds no access to

why: item/trash-view (issue #15): restoring a trashed file from the Trash page must go through FilePolicy::restore() (files.restore plus edit access), and RestoreFile itself checks nothing -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). Without this the Restore control would restore any trashed file for any signed-in user.
expectFailing: refuses to restore a file without edit access

why: item/trash-view (issue #15): purging a trashed file from the Trash page must go through FilePolicy::purge() (files.delete plus manage access), and PurgeFile itself checks nothing -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). Without this the Purge control would permanently delete any trashed file for any signed-in user.
expectFailing: refuses to purge a file without manage access, edit alone is not enough

why: item/trash-view (issue #15): restoring a trashed directory from the Trash page must go through DirectoryPolicy::restore() (directories.manage plus manage access), and RestoreDirectory itself checks nothing -- actions never authorise (CLAUDE.md). MEMBER_PERMISSIONS carries no directories.manage, so without this the Restore control would let an ordinary member with manage-level directory_access alone bring back any subtree cascaded into the trash.
expectFailing: refuses to restore a directory without directories.manage, manage access alone is not enough

why: item/trash-view (issue #15): the trashed FILES listing must be narrowed to directories the viewer can reach (live or trashed). Without this whereIn(), render() would hand the view every trashed file in the instance, which is precisely the query-level leak the doneWhen names -- a view-side @if could hide the row from the rendered HTML, but the data would already have left the query with another user's trashed file in it.
expectFailing: never lists another user's trashed file, asserted against the query result itself

why: item/trash-view (issue #15): the trashed DIRECTORIES listing must be narrowed to the ids viewableTrashedDirectoryIds() resolved, the same shape as the files query beside it. Without this whereIn(), render() would hand the view every trashed directory in the instance regardless of who may see it.
expectFailing: never lists another user's trashed directory, asserted against the query result itself

why: item/home-dashboard's (issue #16) own doneWhen: recents are filtered by DirectoryAccess in the query. Without this whereIn(), Home would list the most recently updated files across the WHOLE instance, regardless of who may reach them.
expectFailing: never lists another user's file in recents, asserted against the query result itself

why: item/home-dashboard (issue #16, folding issue #140): spec 10 names BOTH the topbar nav entry and the Files sidebar's pinned entry "Home", so two links on /files read the same to a screen reader. The sidebar entry keeps its visible text and carries aria-label="Home directory", which CONTAINS that visible text so WCAG label-in-name still holds. Remove the attribute and the anchor's accessible name falls back to its text content -- "Home" -- and the collision is back. The doneWhen asks for this shown failing against main first; an entry here is stronger than a one-off demonstration, because guards re-proves it on every CI run rather than once.
expectFailing: has exactly one link on /files with the accessible name "Home"

why: item/search-filters' doneWhen: a filter must be applied inside the query WITH the permission filter still active, never in place of it. The property filter added here is an EXISTS ANDed onto the same WHERE clause as `d.directory_id IN (...)` -- the predicate that scopes every Fts5SearchIndex query to viewableDirectoryIds(). Removing that predicate proves the new filter cannot substitute for it: a property match on a file outside the viewer's reach must still be invisible. (The mutation removes the directory_id predicate's SQL text, which also desyncs the query's placeholder count from $bindings, so it fails loudly rather than silently leaking -- either way the guard's absence is caught.) The removal target is the predicate AND its bindings together, not the SQL fragment alone: both default to empty above it, so deleting the block leaves valid SQL that simply stops restricting by directory and returns unreachable rows. Removing only the fragment would desync the placeholder count from $bindings and fail as a thrown exception, which would prove SQLite counts placeholders rather than that this predicate keeps unreachable documents out.
remove:
$permission = ' AND d.directory_id IN ('.implode(',', array_fill(0, count($viewableDirectoryIds), '?')).')';
        $permissionBindings = array_values($viewableDirectoryIds);
expectFailing: never returns a property-filtered match outside the viewer reach, on FTS5

why: The same guard as fts5-property-filter-keeps-permission-scope, for LikeSearchIndex: the property filter's whereExists() is chained onto the same Eloquent builder as ->whereIn('directory_id', $viewableDirectoryIds), never a query built fresh that could drop it. Removing that whereIn() call leaves the property EXISTS clause as the only restriction, so a property match on a file outside the viewer's reach would come back.
expectFailing: never returns a property-filtered match outside the viewer reach, via the LIKE fallback

why: item/login-by-username (issue #75): App\Actions\Fortify\AuthenticateUser dispatches a login identifier to the `username` column whenever it contains no "@", on the stated invariant that a stored username can never contain one -- usernameRules()'s regex is the ONLY thing that makes that true, since emailRules() requires the opposite. Remove the regex and any string at all becomes a storable username, including one shaped exactly like another account's email; the two lookups are then no longer provably disjoint and login resolution becomes ambiguous by exactly the collision AuthenticateUser's docblock argues is unreachable.
expectFailing: test_registering_a_username_containing_an_at_sign_is_rejected

why: item/login-by-username (issue #75): AuthenticateUser dispatches a login identifier on str_contains($identifier, '@') -- with one it looks up an email, without one a username -- so the dispatch is unambiguous only while the character sets stay disjoint. usernameRules() excludes '@' at both application write paths, but that is a convention each future write path must remember; UserFactory is already a path that validates nothing. This hook is the one nothing can bypass, the same shape as the email fold beside it. Losing it does not merely break a login: a username equal to another account's email would send the typing user to THAT account's row.
expectFailing: refuses to persist a username containing an at sign, whatever wrote it

why: A zip of a directory is the one download that hands over many files at once, and it holds exactly what ONE viewer could reach at the moment the job ran. The download controller therefore authorises on requested_by rather than on the directory's policy, and the two are genuinely different questions: the test gives the other user Manage on the very directory that was archived, so a policy check would let them straight through. Remove the requested_by guard and that test fails -- someone with access to the directory downloads an archive assembled under somebody else's reach.
expectFailing: hands a built archive only to the person who asked for it

why: BuildDirectoryArchive does not authorise -- the caller did that -- but it does SCOPE, which is not the same thing and is not optional. The file list is built from the requester's own reach intersected with the subtree, so a directory holding a branch they cannot enter still yields an archive without it. Remove the whereIn against viewableDirectoryIds() and the subtree alone decides the contents: the sealed branch lands in the zip, and a person who could not open one of those files gets all of them.
expectFailing: leaves out a subtree the requester cannot reach

why: A drop arrives as three integers from the client and the DOM they came from proves nothing, so dropMove() re-resolves the subject and the destination and asks the same policy the Move select asks. The test that proves it uses a MEMBER rather than an admin on purpose: an admin holds directories.view-all, which DirectoryAccess::resolve() answers with Manage on every directory in the instance, so an admin can never demonstrate a refusal for being out of reach. Remove the authorize on the file branch and a viewer drags a file into a directory they cannot open.
expectFailing: refuses a drop into a directory the viewer cannot reach

why: item/admin-users (issue #18): App\Models\User::booting() registers a `deleting` listener that refuses to delete the last holder of `users.manage`. A shipped doccum instance is single-admin by construction -- public signup is off by default, there is no user-create console command, and before this item there was no admin UI -- so the sole administrator could brick the instance from Settings -> Profile, where DeleteUserForm has always deleted the authenticated user with no guard at all. Removing this throw leaves the surrounding `if` intact and valid, so the guard simply stops refusing and the sole administrator is deleted: the test fails on the account being gone, not on a parse error. Registration is in booting() rather than booted() deliberately -- Spatie's HasRoles registers its own `deleting` listener during boot() and unconditionally detaches the role pivot rows (User has no SoftDeletes, so its isForceDeleting() guard clause is false), and listeners fire in registration order, so a listener added in booted() would read a user whose roles were already gone and never refuse anything.
expectFailing: refuses to delete the sole holder of users.manage

why: item/admin-users (issue #18): the admin Users page changes a user's role set through App\Actions\Users\SetUserRoles, and Spatie's syncRoles() writes the pivot table directly -- it fires no Eloquent model event, so User::booting()'s deleting hook (which catches the DELETE case) cannot see a role change at all. This throw is the entire protection for that path: remove it and an operator can leave the sole holder of `users.manage` with a role that does not carry it, through the ordinary admin UI, with no error and no way back in to fix it.
expectFailing: refuses to strip the sole holder of users.manage down to a role with no permission

why: item/admin-roles (issue #19): the admin Roles page changes a ROLE's permission set through App\Actions\Roles\SetRolePermissions, and Spatie's syncPermissions() writes the role_has_permissions pivot table directly -- exactly like SetUserRoles's own syncRoles() call, it fires no Eloquent model event, so nothing else in the application observes this write at all (verified for this item: no model hook, no observer, no listener anywhere sees a permission sync). This throw is therefore the ENTIRE protection for this path, one level more dangerous than the user-role case beside it -- editing one role strips `users.manage` from every user who holds that role at once, not just one account. Remove it and an operator can uncheck users.manage on the admin role through the ordinary admin UI, with no error, and lock themselves and everyone else out with no way back in.
expectFailing: refuses to strip users.manage from a role that is its sole holder

why: item/admin-periods (issue #20): the purge control being disabled in the Blade view is a courtesy to the operator, not a guard -- a Livewire method call reaches /livewire/update directly with whatever payload the client sends, disabled attribute or not. Periods::purgePeriod() re-runs PeriodPurger::plan() itself and must refuse on that FRESH answer. Remove this check and purgePeriod() purges any period whose confirmation text matches its label, even one PeriodPurger::plan() says is not purgeable -- an open period, one still inside its retention window, or one with a file under legal hold.
expectFailing: refuses to purge a period when purgeable is false even though the request asks for it

why: item/admin-periods (issue #20): the confirmation text field is the only thing standing between a purgeable period and an irreversible delete, so it must be compared to the fresh plan's exact label with a strict comparison. Remove this check and purgePeriod() purges a purgeable period with no confirmation at all -- an empty string, or any other text, purges it just as well as the correct label typed exactly.
expectFailing: refuses to purge a period when the confirmation text does not exactly equal the label

why: issue #185: LedgerValidator::idErrors() used to open with a duplicate-@id check that could never fire, because it iterated $nodes -- a PHP array keyed by @id, whose keys are unique by construction. The real duplicate was destroyed one step earlier, in collectAndCheckStructure(), where a second node sharing an @id silently overwrote the first at $nodes[$id] = [...]. Two items were duplicated in docs/ledger/ledger.jsonld on main, undetected, for exactly this reason. Remove this guard and a second node reusing an @id is once again absorbed into $nodes with no trace, which is what let that happen.
expectFailing: flags a node that redefines an id already used by an earlier node

why: issue #161: EnsureEmailIsVerified gates on the MustVerifyEmail CONTRACT, not the trait User already gets from Authenticatable -- `$request->user() instanceof MustVerifyEmail` was false for every user because the contract was commented out of the model, so the `verified` middleware let every unverified user straight through every route it guards, including four tests in EmailVerificationTest.php that passed while it gated nothing. Remove the contract from the implements clause and the gate goes back to enforcing nothing, exactly as it shipped.
expectFailing: test_an_unverified_user_is_redirected_away_from_a_verified_route

why: issue #161: App\Livewire\Settings\Profile::showDeleteUser() hides the delete-account button for an unverified user, but hiding a control is a courtesy, not a guard, when the action it hides is still reachable directly -- Livewire::test('settings.delete-user-form') reaches deleteUser() with no button in between. Without this check an unverified user (including one who just changed their own email, the exact case this item's design creates) could still delete their account.
expectFailing: test_an_unverified_user_cannot_delete_their_account

why: issue #153, half two: a missing object is permanent, so ExtractText::handle() must stop immediately rather than spend $tries/$backoff retrying bytes that are never coming back. $this->fail($e) is what makes that terminal AND visible -- it marks the job failed and deletes it from the queue from inside handle(), then invokes failed() with the SAME exception so file_texts.error names the missing object rather than whatever failure happens to hit next. Remove it (with the return that stops execution alongside it) and the catch swallows ObjectMissingFromStorage silently: $path is left unassigned, and the job falls through into extracting from an undefined path -- PlainTextExtractor::extract(string $path, ...) is declare(strict_types=1), so that throws a TypeError instead, which escapes handle() uncaught and propagates out of dispatchSync() rather than being caught and settled the way a missing object must be.
expectFailing: treats a missing object as terminal instead of spending its retry budget on it
